title: The Apocalypse, again
tomorrow: violet, white, green, red: why does a church keep changing colors?

lines: BEHOLD, I MAKE ALL THINGS NEW.
cards: Disaster movies end in the dust: a skyline in ruins, a few survivors squinting at the sky. The Apocalypse looks like it's heading there too. A dragon, beasts, plagues, a great city falling.
Then, near the very end, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And he that sat on the throne, said: Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things. All things, new.

teach.h: THE END OF TIME, OR RIGHT NOW?
teach.b: So what is this book about: the end of time, or right now? Catholic readers lean both ways, and each side has a strong case. Some read it first as a book of the last things.
History is going somewhere. Evil doesn't get the final word, and one day God will wipe away every tear and make a new heaven and a new earth.
On that reading, the book is a promise about the future, and its hope is something to wait for. Others read it first as a letter to its own day.
It opens with messages to seven real churches, under pressure, some of them tired, some compromised. Its beasts point to the powers those churches were facing.
And its scenes of heaven, crowds singing holy, holy, holy around the throne and the Lamb, sound like worship, the cry that still echoes at every Mass.
On that reading, the new creation has already begun, and Catholics step into it at the altar. The Church keeps both on the table.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the book's first word in Greek is apokalypsis, and the Douay translates it revelation, an unveiling. The book's own name for itself isn't doom.
And behind it, all things new.

how: Catholics hear the Apocalypse (often called Revelation) read at Mass in the Easter season and at the end of the Church's year, and sing its song of holy, holy, holy in the Sanctus.

games.q: your study group splits on the Apocalypse. you say it's mostly about the end of time. what's the other side's best case?
o: it was written to struggling churches then, and its hope is lived now, at every Mass.
it's a secret code for working out exact dates of the end.
it's only poetry and has nothing to say to faith at all.
games.why: both readings have Catholic readers: a promise for the future, and a letter to its own day whose worship still happens at Mass. the Church keeps both.

practice: Write down one thing that needs making new: a friendship, a street, a habit, a part of you. Under it, write the words behold, I make all things new.
Sit with the page through the sit, hoping for that one thing, and for nothing bigger.
